title: Neighbors Who Cheered
sum: Before the long speeches against Tyre and Egypt, Ezekiel is sent to four small neighbors: Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia. Each is charged with the same wrong in different words. When Jerusalem and its Temple fell, they cheered, took their revenge, or said that Judah was nothing special. Each answer is short and built the same way: 'Because you...', 'therefore I...', and the closing line, 'Then they will know that I am the LORD.'

The four oracles carry no date. They sit here because of their subject, not their day. Their first hearers were the exiles at Tel-abib, not the neighbors, who never heard them. For people who had lost a Temple and a land, they said that every cheer had been noticed.
readings: Read as history

The four nations did act against Judah in the years around 586 BC: Ammon sheltered Ishmael, who killed Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40-41); Edom is accused of looting and of handing over fugitives (Obadiah 10-14); Philistine cities had old grudges. The oracles promise that each will be ended, and the later history of all four, which ends with their names fading, is read as the result.
Read as a lesson about gloating

The charge is not that these nations fought Judah, but that they rejoiced. Clapping, stamping and 'Aha!' (25:3, 6) are the sin. The chapter says that joy at another's ruin, especially at the ruin of God's house, is a crime the LORD answers himself.
Read as part of a set of seven

With Tyre, Sidon and Egypt (chapters 26-32), these four make seven nations in chapters 25-32 (Mount Seir in chapter 35 is a further oracle on the usual count). Babylon, the real destroyer, has no oracle in Ezekiel at all. Seven suggests completeness: the whole circle of Israel's neighbors, with no one left outside God's judgment, except the nation he used.

views.H: Josephus reports that in his twenty-third year, about 582 BC, Nebuchadnezzar campaigned in Syria and subdued the Ammonites and Moabites (Antiquities 10.181). Edom's land was taken over by Arab tribes and then the Nabateans; the Philistine cities lost their kings under Babylon (Ashkelon fell in 604 BC). Whether this is the exact fulfilment Ezekiel meant is a reading; the text names no date.
views.C: Each oracle follows the pattern of a prophetic judgment speech: the charge ('because') and the sentence ('therefore'). Many scholars think the four were gathered, by Ezekiel or an editor, to form a block of seven with Tyre, Sidon and Egypt; others see them as spoken at the time of the siege. The Greek has some differences, such as no 'Seir' in 25:8.
views.J: Later Jewish writers read 'Edom' as Rome, and so read 25:12-14 as a promise about Rome's end.
views.X: Christians read these oracles beside Romans 12:19, where Paul tells believers to leave vengeance to God. Ezekiel 25:14 sets vengeance in Israel's hand 'as my anger and my rage demand', but only as God's instrument. The wrong that Ezekiel names, delight at another's fall, is the one Proverbs 24:17 warns against.
views.F: Some readers expect a final judgment on Ammon, Moab and Edom at the end of the age (Isaiah 11:14; Daniel 11:41), and some prophecy writers match them to modern Jordan. The chapter names no modern state, and its oracles are tied to the exile.

deep.h: Why these four, in this order?
deep.b:
Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia are Israel's near neighbors on the east, south and west. They are not in any strict order of distance. They are also the nations named together in Amos 1-2 and Jeremiah 48-49. Ezekiel's list is shorter, and it leaves out Damascus and Arabia. It is built around one charge: how they behaved when Jerusalem fell.

The Hebrew word for 'vengeance' (naqam) runs through the Edom and Philistine oracles (25:12-17) and is used for both the sin and the sentence. God answers revenge with a revenge of his own, so the sin returns on the sinner. Ezekiel does not say that the neighbors were wrong to defend themselves, only that they took pleasure in Judah's fall and acted on old hatreds.

None of the four peoples is likely to have heard them. Prophets in Israel spoke oracles against foreign nations to their own people, or sent them in writing, as Jeremiah did to the envoys in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:1-11) and to Babylon (Jeremiah 51:59-64). Ezekiel is told to 'fix your face' on a nation, which is a prophet's gesture, but he does it before the exiles. For them the message was practical: the neighbors who profited from Judah's fall were not safe, and the LORD had not lost control.

deep.h: Which witnesses were read for Ezekiel 25-28
deep.b: The Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), read through the site's Hebrew text. The Greek is Swete's printing of Codex Vaticanus, and "the Greek" in these chapters means that text. Dead Sea transcriptions were checked with the Abegg, Bowley and Cook text, and no scroll preserves any verse of chapters 25-28. Ziegler's critical edition of the Greek and Papyrus 967 were not read. Rashi, Radak and the Targum are cited as they appear on Sefaria.

echoes: Amos 1:6-2:3; Jeremiah 48:1-49:22; Zephaniah 2:4-11; Obadiah 10-14; Isaiah 15-16; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 21:28-32; Ezekiel 35:1-15; Romans 12:19; Proverbs 24:17

settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, who hear Ezekiel speak about Ammon; the Ammonites themselves are not present. The book sets Ezekiel among the exiles in Babylon; some scholars think part of his work was done in Jerusalem, and this card does not settle it
settings.when: Undated. The charge assumes the Temple has been profaned and the land laid waste, so after or around the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC
settings.why: To tell the exiles that Ammon's cheering had been heard, and that the land of a people who gloated would be taken by desert herders. It answers the exiles' fear that their neighbors had won.
settings.readers: Later readers, in exile and after the return, found in it a guarantee that the nations that rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall would not have the last word.

settings.when: Undated, from the same period as the other three
settings.why: To answer the claim that Judah was 'the same as all the nations', which denied that the LORD was different from Moab's god Chemosh. The answer is shown in Moab's towns being opened to invasion.
settings.readers: Exiles who were tempted to say that the LORD was one god among many.

settings.to: The exiles, about Edom, Judah's kin
settings.why: To say that Edom's revenge, taking the chance to settle old quarrels with its brother nation, would be repaid by Israel's hand. Edom's betrayal hurt most because it was family.
views: Some readers see Judas Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 5:3) and John Hyrcanus's conquest of Idumea (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257-258) as the 'hand of my people Israel'.
Others read the line as a promise whose fulfilment the text leaves open, as chapter 35 returns to Edom.

settings.to: The exiles, about the Philistine cities
settings.why: To name an 'old hatred' as the source of Philistine cruelty and to say that its record would end. The Philistines were Israel's oldest enemy, and the oracle closes the list of neighbors.

title: The Doors of the Peoples
sum: Tyre, the sea-trading queen of Phoenicia, cheered when Jerusalem fell, because the broken city meant business for her. Dated to the eleventh year (587/586 BC), the oracle answers with an army from the north, led by Nebuchadnezzar, and then with the sea itself. Walls fall, streets are trampled and the stones are dumped in the water. The island city becomes a bare rock where fishermen spread nets.

The chapter then turns to the mourners. The princes of the sea come down from their thrones and sit trembling on the ground. They sing a funeral song for the city of praise. The last picture goes beneath the waves: Tyre is sent down to the Pit among the dead of long ago, while the LORD sets splendor in the land of the living.
readings: Read as a forecast of Alexander

Many Christian readers see 26:4, 12 and 14 as a precise forecast: the mainland city scraped bare, its stones thrown into the sea for Alexander's causeway in 332 BC. They point out that the island city was left a rock for fishermen for long periods.
Read as the end of a power

Other readers hold that the oracle is about Tyre's pride and trade empire, under a series of invaders, which really ended. The city was not 'never rebuilt', and Ezekiel 29:17-20 says Nebuchadnezzar's siege gained little, so the oracle is not a literal timetable.
Read as a warning to the proud

Any reading must note the charge: Tyre's 'Aha!' was commercial. The sin is to turn another's disaster into profit. The chapter is the first of three speeches against Tyre, and it ends, like the next two, in the Pit.

views.H: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the 580s and 570s BC (Josephus, Against Apion 1.156, from Menander); Ezekiel says in 29:17-20 that it did not pay. Alexander took the island city in 332 BC after seven months and a causeway; Tyre was rebuilt, and remained a major city through Roman times.
views.C: Scholars date the oracle to the eleventh year but note the missing month and the problem that Ezekiel does not hear of the fall until 33:21. The shift from 'he' (Nebuchadnezzar, 26:7-11) to 'they' (26:12) and 'many nations' (26:3) is noticed by readers on both sides of the fulfillment debate (Swete's Greek keeps 'he' in 26:12). The lament in verses 17-18 is in the qinah meter.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the siege of verses 7-11 as Nebuchadnezzar's, as the text says. Rashi, on Sefaria, comments on 26:12 only to gloss the word 'your merchandise', and Sefaria has no comment of his on 26:14.
views.X: Christian readers have often taken Tyre as a type of worldly power and wealth, as Revelation 18 does for Babylon. The apologetic argument from Alexander's causeway is a modern use of the chapter.
views.F: A few futurist readers see Tyre's fall as a type of the fall of 'Babylon the Great' in Revelation 18, which borrows Ezekiel's merchants, ships and mourners; the oracle itself is dated to the sixth century BC.

deep.h: Tyre: a city on a rock
deep.b:
Tyre stood on an island about 600 meters off the coast, with a settlement on the mainland facing it. Its colonies reached Cyprus, North Africa (Carthage) and Spain. It ruled through trade and its fleet, and its patron god was Melqart. Kings of Tyre, from Hiram the friend of David and Solomon (1 Kings 5:1-12) to Ittobaal in Ezekiel's day, grew rich on sea trade. Assyria had besieged and taxed the city; Nebuchadnezzar did the same. In 332 BC Alexander took it after seven months by building a causeway.

Ezekiel's three speeches on Tyre (26, 27, 28) are among the longest oracles against any one city in the Bible. Isaiah 23 is a shorter parallel, with a different ending: there Tyre is restored and its profits become holy.

This is among the most-argued fulfillment questions in the Bible. Four positions:

Exact: the mainland city was destroyed and its rubble was thrown into the sea by Alexander (Curtius 4.2.18; Diodorus 17.40). The island was then left as a place for nets. Peter Stoner's Science Speaks counted this as one of many 'probability' fulfilments.

Partial and progressive: the verbs in 26:4 and 26:12 are plural ('they') in the Hebrew (the Greek of 26:12 is singular), so the oracle describes a series of invaders (Babylon, Persia, Greece), with Alexander the last and most thorough.

Conditional or figurative: 'never built again' (26:14) means the end of Tyre as a world power. Tyre was rebuilt, and Paul found disciples there (Acts 21:3-6).

Failed and corrected: Ezekiel himself says in 29:17-20 that Nebuchadnezzar did not get his wages from Tyre. A prophet who admits this did not read his own words as a mechanical timetable.

echoes: Isaiah 23:1-18; Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9-10; Zechariah 9:3-4; 1 Kings 5:1-12; Ezekiel 27:1-36; Ezekiel 28:1-19; Ezekiel 29:17-20; Matthew 11:21-22; Revelation 18:9-19

settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, about Tyre; Tyre is addressed in the second person but is not present
settings.when: The first day of an unnamed month in the eleventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, 587/586 BC, around the fall of Jerusalem. The eleventh year runs from spring 587 to spring 586 BC, so the oracle may come before the fall of the city (the fourth month, Jeremiah 52:6) as well as after it
settings.why: To say that Tyre's delight at Jerusalem's fall was a crime, and that the sea city would be broken by the same Babylonian army that had broken Jerusalem. For the exiles, who feared that Tyre had won, it showed the LORD as master of the nations.
settings.readers: Later readers saw in the chapter the pattern for all great commercial powers; Revelation 18 uses it for Babylon.
views: The date falls in the year Jerusalem fell, and Tyre's 'Aha!' may be a quotation of what Tyre was already saying about the siege.
The words 'now that she lies waste' suggest news of the fall had arrived, which fits the order of events in 33:21 only if the news came earlier than the book's own account.

settings.what: The islands mourn Tyre; Tyre goes down to the Pit
settings.when: The same oracle, as its second part
settings.why: To show Tyre's fall as seen from outside, in the shaking of its allies, and then from below, in the world of the dead. The turn to 'the land of the living' tells the exiles that Tyre's end is not their end.

title: The Ship Tyre
sum: Ezekiel is told to sing a funeral song over Tyre, and the song turns the city into a ship. In the first half the ship is built from the best materials of the world: cypress from Hermon, cedar from Lebanon, oaks from Bashan, ivory from Cyprus, linen from Egypt and purple from Elishah. It is crewed by the people of Sidon, Arvad and Byblos and guarded by soldiers from Persia, Lud and Put.

The center of the poem is a trade list of about twenty peoples and what they brought: silver and tin from Tarshish, slaves and bronze from Javan, horses from Togarmah, wheat and balm from Judah. The ship is loaded, glorious and very heavy. Then an east wind breaks it in the heart of the seas. Sailors and kings stand on the shore with dust on their heads, singing: 'Who was ever like Tyre?'
readings: Read as a map of the ancient world

The trade list (27:12-24) is the longest list of commercial goods and trading partners in the Bible, with many of the same names as the Table of Nations in Genesis 10. It is a source for historians of Phoenician trade.
Read as an allegory of pride
The ship says, 'I am complete in beauty' (27:3). The poem gives every reason for the boast, and then drowns it. The weight that makes the ship glorious is the weight that sinks her (27:25).
Read as a pattern for Babylon

Revelation 18 borrows the merchants, the cargoes, the shipmasters and the dust on the head for the fall of Babylon the Great. Tyre becomes the standing example of an economy built on luxury and on the trade in human lives (27:13; Revelation 18:13).

views.H: The trade list reflects Tyre in the early sixth century BC, with Judah and Israel selling grain, oil and balm, as in 1 Kings 5:11 and Acts 12:20. Persians, Lydians and Libyans appear as hired soldiers.
views.C: Scholars treat the chapter as a long qinah, a funeral song, in two or three parts: the ship (3-11), the trade (12-25a) and the wreck (25b-36). Some scholars think the trade list was an existing document that Ezekiel used. The Greek differs in many names, which shows uncertainty about the place names already when it was made.
views.J: The Greek, made by Jewish translators in Egypt, translates several place names in its own way (Carthaginians for Tarshish, Rhodians for Dedan), which shows the list was already hard to read in antiquity.
views.X: Christian readers take the chapter, with Revelation 18, as a warning about wealth built on others' suffering. The mention of 'human lives' is the line that Revelation 18:13 repeats.
views.F: Futurist readers who link Tyre with the end-time Babylon of Revelation 17-18 draw on this chapter for the picture of a final world economy and its fall; this is a reading of Revelation, not of Ezekiel's own date.

deep.h: A catalogue of the known world
deep.b:
The trade list names about two dozen peoples and places, from Spain (Tarshish) to Arabia (Sheba, Raamah, Kedar) and from Anatolia (Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah) to Judah. It follows no single route. Some names are the same as in the Table of Nations: Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah, Dedan, Sheba, Raamah, Elishah, Kittim. The ship is, in effect, the world of Genesis 10 put to work for one city.

The Greek differs a good deal. It reads Tarshish as Carthage, Dedan as Rhodes, Put as Libya, Zahar as Miletus. Some of these are interpretations of names the translators no longer recognized, and some may reflect another Hebrew text; the variants record the clearest cases.

Two items in the list are people: 'human lives' (27:13) and, by implication, the sailors and soldiers hired from many lands. The prophets Joel and Amos both charge Tyre with trading in captives (Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9-10). Ezekiel does not repeat the charge in this chapter, but 28:16 says that violence filled the king through his trade.

Revelation 18:13 ends its list of Babylon's cargo with the same phrase. The Greek expression is the same in both books, in different cases (en psychais anthropon in Ezekiel, psychas anthropon in Revelation). Readers can hardly miss the link between fine goods and cruel trade.

echoes: Isaiah 23:1-18; Psalm 48:7; Jonah 1:1-16; Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9-10; Genesis 10:2-7; 1 Kings 5:1-12; Revelation 18:9-19

settings.what: A lament for Tyre as a wrecked ship
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel, who is told to 'raise a lament'
settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, hearing a song addressed to Tyre; the lament is addressed to the city but is performed before Ezekiel's own people
settings.when: Undated; it follows the dated oracle of 26:1 and is usually taken to be from the same period (about 587/586 BC)
settings.why: To give the exiles a song to sing over the city that had cheered at their fall. A funeral song is for the dead, and singing it early says that the end is certain. The long list of Tyre's glory is there to show how large the fall will be.
settings.readers: Readers in the Second Temple period and in the early church read the poem as a pattern for the fall of any proud trading power, as Revelation 18 does.

title: A God in the Heart of the Seas
sum: The chapter has four parts. First the ruler of Tyre, who says, 'I am a god, I sit in a seat for gods,' is told that he is a human being, and that outsiders will bring him down to the Pit. Then Ezekiel is told to sing a lament over the king of Tyre. The king is described as the seal of a pattern, full of wisdom, in Eden, the garden of God, covered with precious stones, a cherub on the holy mountain, without blame until wrong was found in him. Because of trade and violence he is profaned, thrown to the ground, burned from within and left as ash.

The last two parts are short. Sidon, north of Tyre, is told 'I am against you.' And the chapter ends with the promise to Israel: no more thorns from hostile neighbors, a gathering from the peoples, and houses and vineyards in safety. The section on the nations turns on Israel's safe settlement.
readings: Read as a human king described in Eden's colors

The king is the Tyrian ruler of Ezekiel's day, or the line of Tyrian kings. The poet uses an Eden story to say how far he fell: from the rank of a priest-king in God's garden, covered with jewels, to a man thrown down and burned. The details are meant to flatter, then to wound.
Read as a being behind the king

Some Christian readers, from Tertullian (about AD 208) on, have taken verses 12-19 as describing the fall of a created being, Satan or a rebel angel, whose pride and expulsion lie behind the king of Tyre. The Eden setting, the cherub and the words 'from the day you were created' are the main reasons given.
Read as a retold myth

Critical scholars read the poem as Ezekiel's use of an older Near Eastern picture of a primal figure on the mountain of the gods. The Hebrew and Greek texts differ on whether he is the cherub himself or is placed with the cherub, which suggests the story was told more than one way.

views.H: The ruler is probably Ittobaal of Tyre, king during Nebuchadnezzar's siege (Josephus, Against Apion 1.156). 'Outsiders, the most violent of the nations' (28:7) are the Babylonians. Sidon's later destruction by Persia (Diodorus 16.41-45) can be set beside 28:22-23.
views.C: The two speeches differ in form: 28:1-10 is a judgment speech in prose, and 28:11-19 is a poem, a lament (qinah). Many critics treat verses 12-19 as built on a tradition of a primal man or king in a garden on a mountain, which Ezekiel adapted. The Hebrew and the Greek differ in verses 12, 13, 14 and 16.
views.J: Rashi, on Sefaria, takes the king as a historical ruler, links the holy mountain with the Temple mount and the king with the cedar sent to Solomon, and reads the 'seat of God' (28:2) as a heaven-like structure built over the sea. Radak, on 28:12, explains 'Eden, the garden of God' as abundance and luxury, quoting the Targum, and does not name the king there. A rabbinic list in Derekh Eretz Zuta 1 counts Hiram of Tyre among nine who entered the Garden of Eden alive.
views.X: Tertullian and Origen read verses 12-19 of a fallen spiritual being; Gregory the Great sets the nine stones of 28:13 beside the nine orders of angels (Homily 34 on the Gospels), and the Scofield Reference Bible teaches it. Others read the passage of a human king and base the doctrine of Satan's fall on other texts such as Luke 10:18, 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6 and Revelation 12:7-9.
views.F: In dispensational teaching, verses 12-19 are often read of Satan, as a window on his pre-Eden glory and his final judgment. Revelation 20:10 gives the end of the devil in fire; Ezekiel 28:18 has a fire from within.

deep.b:
Verses 1-10 are addressed to the nagid, the ruler, and verses 11-19 to the melekh, the king. The first is prose and ends with the ruler dying 'the death of the uncircumcised'. The second is a poem and ends with the king as ash before the eyes of all. They are tied by repeated words: wisdom (28:3, 4, 5, 7, 12, 17), your heart grew proud (28:2, 5, 17), trading (28:5, 16, 18), and the word profane (28:7, 16, 18). The Greek of Codex Vaticanus calls both men archon, 'ruler'.

Whether the same man is meant, or the ruler is the living man and the king the office and its traditions, is not settled. What is clear is that the second speech goes further than the first: the ruler claims divinity and is told he is human; the king is described as something close to divine and is told what happened to him.

deep.h: What the lament says, line by line
deep.b:
The poem has about nine claims, and any reading must deal with all of them. The king (1) was a seal on a pattern, full of wisdom and complete in beauty; (2) was in Eden, the garden of God; (3) was covered with nine precious stones; (4) was created, and the gems were ready on the day of his creation; (5) was a cherub (Hebrew), the one who covers; (6) was placed on the holy mountain of God and walked among stones of fire; (7) was without blame from his creation until wrong was found in him; (8) was filled with violence through trade, and sinned; (9) was profaned, driven from the mountain, thrown to the ground, shown to kings, and burned by a fire from within.

Nothing here mentions a serpent, a tree, a woman, rebellion in heaven, or the name Satan. Genesis 2-3 has no gem-covered figure, no mountain and no cherub in the garden itself (the cherubim come at the east gate afterward, Genesis 3:24), though Havilah has gold and onyx (Genesis 2:11-12). Isaiah 14:12-15, which is often tied to this passage, has a king who wants to climb to the heavens, which Ezekiel 28 does not say.

Zimmerli, Greenberg, Block and many other commentators read the lament as addressed to a human king of Tyre throughout. The speech begins, 'Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre', and it ends with the king's body as ash 'before the eyes of all who looked at you', in the sight of the nations. Ezekiel uses Eden language of human rulers elsewhere: Assyria is a cedar in Eden, and Egypt's trees are in the garden of God (Ezekiel 31:8-9, 16-18). The poem sets Tyre's claim to divine wisdom against the story of the first human who was set in a garden and lost it.

The strongest reasons are the context (the whole of chapters 26-28 is about the real city), the nature of the charge (trade and violence, 28:16, 18, which are human sins) and Ezekiel's habit of addressing living rulers in mythic images. The objection is that no human king was 'created' blameless on the mountain of God, so the poem must be using a story, not describing a biography.

The reading is old. Tertullian (about AD 208) says in Against Marcion that in the person of the prince of Tyre the prophecy is spoken against the devil (book 2, chapter 10). Origen, in On First Principles (book 1, chapter 5), argues that Ezekiel 28 and Isaiah 14 point to an opposing power that was once holy and happy and fell. Gregory the Great, in his Homily 34 on the Gospels, reads the nine stones of verse 13 as the nine orders of angels with which the first angel was adorned, and the idea passed into the Western tradition. The Scofield Reference Bible of 1909 states it as a teaching, and most dispensational writers have followed.

The reading rests on the features that a human life does not fit: Eden, the cherub, the creation 'on the day', the mountain of God, the blamelessness until a flaw appeared, and the expulsion. Its supporters add Luke 10:18 and Revelation 12:9, in which a fall from heaven is told of Satan.

The objections are that the text never names Satan, that the context names the king of Tyre, that the 'violence in trade' is a human sin, that the Greek makes the cherub a separate being (so the king is not the cherub), and that the tie to Satan is made by readers and is not in the poem itself. Those who hold the human-king reading may still hold that Satan fell, on other texts.

The medieval Jewish commentators read the king as a historical figure. Rashi, in the Sefaria text, takes the 'holy mountain of God' as the Temple mount and connects the king with the cedar sent to Solomon, so that the lament is for a king of Tyre in the line of Hiram; he reads the 'seat of God' of 28:2 as a heaven-like structure the king built over the sea. Radak reads 'Eden, the garden of God' as a figure for luxury and plenty, quoting the Targum's rendering of abundance, and takes the 'tambourines and sockets' as instruments; in his comment on 28:12 he does not name the king.

Rabbinic legend ties a Tyrian king to the garden in another way: Derekh Eretz Zuta 1, in the Sefaria text, lists Hiram of Tyre among nine people who entered the Garden of Eden alive (a footnote says that 'king' may have crept in). That is a story about Hiram, not a reading of Ezekiel 28 as Adam.

deep.h: How the Greek changes the picture
deep.b: The oldest Greek that survives, in Codex Vaticanus as Swete printed it, calls the king archon, 'ruler' (28:12). Instead of 'perfect in beauty' it has 'a crown of beauty'. It has twelve stones, the same twelve, in the same order, as the Greek of Exodus 28:17-20, with silver and gold added; the three the Hebrew lacks are exactly the breastpiece's third row. In verse 14 it reads 'from the day you were created with the cherub I set you', so the king and the cherub are two beings. In verse 16 it reads 'you were wounded from the mountain of God, and the cherub led you out', so the cherub is the one who removes him. In verse 18 it has God, not the king, profaning the sanctuaries. These changes make the king more human and the cherub more like an angelic guardian.

The story of a proud angel who falls is not told in the Hebrew Bible. It grows in the Second Temple period from Genesis 6, from Isaiah 14 (where the Latin Vulgate's Lucifer, 'light-bringer', renders the Hebrew 'Shining One'), and from stories like the one in the Life of Adam and Eve (chapters 12-16), where Satan is cast down for refusing to bow to Adam. The New Testament has the fall of Satan in Luke 10:18, Revelation 12:7-9 and the angels who sinned in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6. The church fathers who tie Ezekiel 28 to this story are joining separate threads. That does not make the connection wrong, but it means the connection is made by readers and is not in the poem itself.
deep.refs: Isaiah 14:12-15; Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:7-9; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; Life of Adam and Eve 12-16

deep.h: Why there is no "Where Christians differ" card here
deep.b: A card of that kind sets churches against each other where their teaching conflicts. Here the churches' teaching does not rest on this passage. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (391-393) bases the fall of the angels on Genesis 3, Wisdom 2:24, John 8:44, Revelation 12:9, 2 Peter 2:4, 1 John 3:8 and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), and cites neither Ezekiel 28 nor Isaiah 14. The divide over Ezekiel 28 runs among exegetes, ancient and modern, Jewish and Christian: Tertullian, Origen and Gregory the Great read it of a fallen being; Rashi, Radak, Zimmerli, Greenberg and Block read a human king; dispensational teachers use it for Satan. That is set out in the readings above, as views, and not as a conflict between traditions.

The verb chalal, 'profane', occurs three times in the two speeches, and in the Hebrew each time with a different subject. Outsiders profane the king's splendor (28:7). God profanes the king and removes him from the mountain (28:16). The king profanes his own sanctuaries (28:18). So the fall has a human cause, a divine cause and a moral cause, and none cancels the others: a reader does not have to choose between 'God did it', 'Babylon did it' and 'he did it to himself'. Giving divine and human causes together is a familiar feature of Ezekiel's judgments. The pattern depends on the Hebrew: Swete's Greek has 'I profaned your sanctuaries' at 28:18, so God is the subject twice and the king never.

echoes: Genesis 2:8-3:24; Isaiah 14:12-15; Exodus 28:17-20; Daniel 11:36-37; Acts 12:20-23; 2 Thessalonians 2:4; Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:7-9; Revelation 21:19-20; Ezekiel 31:8-18

settings.what: Oracle to the ruler of Tyre
settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, about the ruler (nagid) of Tyre, who is addressed but is not present
settings.when: Undated; it is placed after the dated oracle of 26:1 by the order of the chapters only, so about 587/586 BC or soon after is a guess from that order
settings.why: To answer the ruler's claim to be a god. The exiles had seen Babylon's kings treated as gods. They needed to hear that a king who calls himself a god is a human being, and that the most powerful rulers die like anyone else.
settings.readers: Later readers saw in the ruler the type of every human ruler who claims divine honors (Isaiah 14; Daniel 11; Acts 12; 2 Thessalonians 2).

settings.what: Lament for the king of Tyre
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel, who is told to 'raise a lament'
settings.to: The exiles, hearing a funeral song for a king; the king himself is not present
settings.why: To set the king's fall in the largest frame the exiles knew, the story of Eden and the mountain of God. They hear that pride and violent trade, not weakness in their God, were the reasons for the fall of a king.
settings.readers: Christian and Jewish readers across the centuries read the lament as a window on a primal fall; whether it is a window on Adam, on a human king or on Satan is the question in the chapter notes.
views: The listeners are exiles hearing a prophet's mocking lament for a living ruler, in the language of their own Eden story.
The listeners are given a view of a fall that happened before history, which the king of Tyre repeats.

settings.why: To finish the circle of Israel's neighbors on the north with a short word and no named charge. Sidon is judged so that the LORD may show himself holy before the nations.

settings.to: The exiles, who have lost the land and live among the nations
settings.when: Undated; it closes the first set of oracles against the nations and looks forward to the return
settings.why: To tell the exiles what the judgments on their neighbors are for. When the nations around them fall, Israel will have no more thorns in its side, will be gathered from the peoples, and will live in safety in the land given to Jacob.
settings.readers: Exiles and later readers returning to the land found in it the reason that the nations' judgment is part of Israel's hope.
